title: The Challenges of Implementing Knowledge Management Systems
description: This discussion explores the scope of knowledge management, moving beyond simple acquisition systems to encompass diverse resources and domain-specific workflows. It highlights the gap between installing knowledge management technology and ensuring users successfully adapt and integrate new systems into existing, often flexible, organizational processes.
summary:
The discussion introduces knowledge management (KM) from a technical perspective, noting that KM involves various resource types such as text, media, software, processes, and reports, all operating within domain-specific workflows.

Traditionally, knowledge management has been viewed as a knowledge acquisition system, involving users filling out forms and storing data within document management systems (DMS). The primary goal of KM is retention—ensuring knowledge persists when employees leave or retire.

However, a major challenge arises during implementation: technologists install KM systems, but users must then adapt through education and new quality management procedures. The core issue is that workflows are often defined by social convention rather than being strictly defined by the system itself, meaning rules can be deviated from when necessary, especially in knowledge-intensive enterprises.

title: Kiwi: A Semantic Knowledge Management Platform
description: Kiwi is a platform that integrates knowledge management philosophy and wiki flexibility with the Semantic Web to create a system for building social software applications. It uses machine-readable links and rule-based reasoning to provide advanced, personalized search and structured knowledge retrieval.
summary: The presentation introduced Kiwi, a platform developed through an EU-funded research project, designed for Enterprise Knowledge Management (EKM). Kiwi combines the flexibility of a wiki philosophy with the power of the Semantic Web, creating a system that links human content with machine-readable metadata. The platform is built on Java Enterprise Edition and is designed to handle diverse content types, such as meeting minutes and location data, by using flexible ontologies instead of rigid databases. Key features include automatic semantic extraction of links and entities, sophisticated tagging (free text and conceptual), and rule-based reasoning (e.g., identifying a "located meeting" based on location and event data). This system supports metadata synchronization, allowing human-written content to be seamlessly updated with machine data. Advanced functionalities include personalized search, faceted searching based on both textual and RDF properties, and an experimental query language. Ultimately, Kiwi aims to serve as a unified access point for content and metadata, facilitating enterprise integration and serving as a foundation for future applications.

title: The Kiwi Project Key System and Community Resources
description: This segment focuses on the vision behind the Kiwi system—creating adaptable technology—and highlights the key system prototype, team involvement, and the available resources and community opportunities for collaboration.
summary: The speaker emphasizes that the most interesting part of the presentation is the demonstration of the actual key system prototype, which serves as a research prototype. The core philosophy is that technology and organization must be adaptable to people. The project relies on a collaborative team effort, stressing that involvement is distributed across multiple contributors. The speaker mentions a recent release party in Vienna where key developers were present. Key resources are provided via the official Kiwi Project website (for administrative info), the Planet Key Block (for articles), and a crucial Community page. This Community page provides access to all documentation, software downloads, and a demo. For potential collaborators, the speaker also mentions the opportunity to join the Salzburg New Media Lab in Austria.
